newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Kabila to be told directly to respect human rights.
newsitem.headline: Kabila to be told directly to respect human rights.

text.p: Envoys from at least a dozen countries plan to tell Congo President Laurent Kabila face to face he must do something on human rights and the treatment of Rwandan refugees, diplomats said on Wednesday.

A group of 21 ambassadors, mainly from the United States and Europe but including Canada, Japan, Egypt and South Africa, met at the United Nations after senior U.N. officials asked them to consider what they could do to express their concerns.

Many said their governments would probably send their ambassadors in Kinshasa, capital of the new Democratic Republic of Congo, in one large group to see Kabila before he leaves for the Organisation of African Unity summit in the Zimbabwean capital of Harare this weekend.

Kieran Prendergast, the U.N. undersecretary-general for political affairs, said the ambassadors were asked what they could do quickly "to get across to Mr. Kabila the very deep concerns there are in the international community on the humanitarian and human rights fronts."
He told reporters that the new Congo government, formerly Zaire, "have to acknowledge to themselves at least that there is a problem that needs addressing."
U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan, a Ghanaian, will be at next week's OAU meeting Harare along with his special envoy for Central Africa, Mohammed Sahnoun, an Algerian.

Meanwhile, the Security Council on Wednesday haggled over a U.S.-initiated statement meant to have an impact on the OAU meeting. It would call for protection and security for refugees and express concern about reports of massacres.
The council would also call for the withdrawal of foreign troops, a reference to neighbouring countries whose soldiers and advisers helped Kabila to power.
China so far has hesitated in approving the statement, saying it was interference in Congo's internal affairs.

Victory for Kabila's rebels has brought little prospect of relief for hundreds of thousands of Rwandan Hutu refugees sheltering in the country, some of them involved in the 1994 genocide against minority Tutsis in Rwanda.
Widespread reports of massacres in eastern Zaire, including innocent civiians, have brought unsuccessful appeals for an international probe.

Separately the United States, which is supportive of Kabila, intends to send its U.N. Ambassador Bill Richardson to see Kinsasha after next week's OAU meeting and urge him to form a broad-based government. Richardson said he would also discuss economic issues as well as the plight of the refugees.
